cards.explanation: The answer is creditor, friends. That's a man her husband owed money to, and he's coming to take her two children as his slaves. She cries out to Elisha, the prophet of the LORD, with all of that on her shoulders. I can't imagine a heavier knock on the door.

She has just a jar of oil, friends. She tells Elisha, the prophet, “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” One jar. When someone asks what you've got and the answer is that small, it takes some honesty to say it out loud. I'd have been tempted to dig around in the cabinets for something more impressive.

The answer is empty jars, friends! Elisha, the prophet, tells her, “borrow empty jars from all your neighbors.” Think about it. A woman with one jar of oil gets sent out to collect a pile of jars with nothing in them. I think that is a strange shopping list, and it makes you wonder what comes next.

The answer is False, friends. Elisha, the prophet, says, “Do not gather just a few.” He sends her for empty jars from all her neighbors (2 Kings 4:3). So the plan was never to start small. He wants her collecting big.

The answer is True, friends. When all the jars were full, she asked her son for another, and he replied, “There are no more jars.” Then the oil stopped flowing (2 Kings 4:6). Her sons kept bringing jars and she kept pouring. The oil lasted as long as the jars did.

The blanks are debt and remainder, friends. Elisha says, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt.” That's the very trouble she cried out about at the start, the creditor coming to take her children. Then he says, “Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” That means money is left over after the debt is paid, so she and her sons can live on what's left.

The answer is False, friends. Verse 8 says, “…whenever he would pass by, he would stop there to eat.” Elisha, the prophet, became a regular at her table in Shunem. If I found a house where the table was always set, I'd start taking the long way home too.

The answer is room, friends! She says, “Please let us make a small room upstairs and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for him.” She says this to her husband after she sees that Elisha, the prophet, is a holy man of God. A bed and a table and a lamp. That's a thoughtful thing to give a guest.

The answer is False, friends. Elisha, the prophet, is the one who makes the offer, asking whether he can speak on her behalf to the king or the commander of the army. Her reply is, “I have a home among my own people…” A word with the king is quite an offer, and that's the answer she gives.

The answer is that she has no son and her husband is old. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “Well, she has no son…” and “…her husband is old.” Elisha asked what should be done for her, and Gehazi had an answer ready. Sometimes the servant is the one who notices.

She asks him not to lie to her, friends. She says, “No, my lord…” and then, “Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” I bet she's being careful with her heart. The text doesn't say why she answered this way.

The answer is True, friends. Verse 17 says, “But the woman did conceive, and at that time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had told her.” Elisha, the prophet, had said it, and it happened on the schedule he gave. She had told him not to lie to her, and she wasn't lied to.

The answer is mother, friends. The father says to a servant, “Carry him to his mother.” The boy had cried out, “My head! My head!” before that. I think this is a hard moment, and I'll just say it plain.

She lays him on the man of God's bed, friends. The text says she “…laid him on the bed of the man of God.” That's the bed in the upstairs room she and her husband had made for Elisha, the prophet. Then she shut the door and went out. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think she's holding it together by doing one step at a time.

She tells him everything is all right, friends. Her husband asks why she's going today, since it's not a New Moon or a Sabbath, and she answers, “Everything is all right…” That's all the text tells us she says. Why she put it that way, the passage doesn't say.

Elisha tells Gehazi to leave her alone, friends. Elisha, the prophet, tells his servant Gehazi, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” Gehazi came to push her away, and Elisha stopped him. Elisha gives his reason in the same breath: her soul is in deep distress.
The answer is False, friends. Elisha, the prophet, says, “…the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” He says her soul is in deep distress, but that the LORD hasn't told him why.

The answer is staff, friends! Elisha tells Gehazi, his servant, “Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go!” Then Gehazi is to lay it on the boy's face. Tie up the garment, grab the staff, and move. That's a man with somewhere to be.

The answer is False, friends. Elisha does not tell Gehazi to greet everyone. Elisha, the prophet, tells Gehazi, his servant, “If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him.” No hellos in either direction, so the instruction is to go.

She tells Elisha she won't leave him, friends. She says, “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” She had already clung to his feet, and now she says it outright. So he got up and followed her.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “…there was no sound or response.” Gehazi, Elisha's servant, went back to meet Elisha and told him, “The boy has not awakened.” This is a heavy moment, and I think it's okay to just sit with it.

He prays to the LORD, friends. The text says Elisha, the prophet, “…went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.” Before anything else happens, he talks to God. That's the order of things.

The answer is warm, friends. The text says, “As he stretched himself out over him, the boy’s body became warm.” Elisha, the prophet, had stretched out on the bed over the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand. That's the first change we see.

The boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes, friends. The text says Elisha, the prophet, stretched himself out over the boy again, “…and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.” Seven times, and the text counts every one. After all that heaviness, I think this is the moment the room changes.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground.” Only then did she pick up her son and go out. I think that says a lot about her heart in that moment, and the text lets her do it without a word.
